I'm looking at this Closure-14b defect4j task, which requires writing a JUnit4 test for ControlFlowAnalysis, a package-private class in com.google.javascript.jscomp that depends on Node and AbstractCompiler from the closure-compiler codebase.

The classpath listed doesn't include a compiler.jar, but since this is Defects4J working against the actual source tree, classes like AbstractCompiler, NodeTraversal, NodeUtil, ControlFlowGraph, Node, and Token will be compiled from the project's own source rather than needing a separate jar -- the listed jars (guava, rhino, etc.) are just supporting libraries.

I'm thinking through how to write a JUnit4 test that exercises ControlFlowAnalysis directly using Node objects, but the challenge is that it depends on AbstractCompiler, an abstract class that needs a real or mocked instance. The typical approach in this project is to instantiate a real Compiler, parse source code to get the Node tree, then run ControlFlowAnalysis.process() on it.

Tracing further, the recursion continues through NAME into the CALL node, which matches the exception case directly and returns true—so the VAR statement does connect to exception handlers, though this depends on assumptions about isEnteringNewCfgNode that I can't verify from source, so I'll flag this as a plausible-but-uncertain test case rather than something I'm fully confident in.

I also want to test isBreakTarget, matchLabel, and isContinueTarget—isBreakStructure is package-private static and callable directly with a properly constructed WHILE node, but isBreakTarget requires the target's parent to have correct label structure, which will be trickier to construct manually.

For isBreakStructure and isContinueStructure, I can construct minimal Node objects directly using Rhino's Node constructor that takes a node type, like `new Node(Token.FOR)` or `new Node(Token.BLOCK)`, assuming that constructor is available in this Closure Compiler fork.

Adding more test cases...

Writing for-in test case...

The label case just recurses into the last child of the LABEL node, so the fall-through target is whatever the body's own fall-through resolves to — I'll write a similar test with a labeled block to confirm that.

I'm confident the standard Closure Node API methods like addChildToBack, getFirstChild, and getLastChild are what's actually used in the source, so I'll rely on those for constructing test trees. For that I need to figure out how to properly navigate the ControlFlowGraph API from outside — whether there's a direct way to get successor nodes for a raw AST node versus needing an internal DiGraphNode wrapper, since that distinction isn't fully clear without seeing more of the dependency source.

Since ControlFlowAnalysisTest lives in the same package, these methods must be at least package-visible, so it's safe to rely on exactly getEntry(), getDirectedSuccNodes(), getDirectedGraphNodes(), and getImplicitReturn() for testing.

This gives me an integration test plan: parse the code, run cfa.process(null, root), grab cfg = cfa.getCfg(), get entry = cfg.getEntry(), then find successors via cfg.getDirectedSuccNodes(entry).

I'll check each successor's getValue() to confirm CFG structure, though I should avoid asserting specific branch labels like ON_TRUE/ON_FALSE since the API for retrieving edge labels alongside successor nodes isn't clearly exposed in what I've seen.

A reasonable simplification is to just verify target nodes are reachable as successors by identity, without distinguishing branches — this still exercises the if/else/while/for/switch/try/break/continue paths since each handleXxx() method calls createEdge exactly once per code path, so triggering each handler with the right AST shape achieves branch coverage.

Mapping this out concretely: handleIf with/without else covers its branch; handleFor with childCount==4 vs not covers its branch; handleSwitch with case, no-case-with-default, and no-case-no-default covers all three; handleCase's three outcomes for next/default lookup; handleTry's various catch scenarios; break/continue traversal through finally blocks; connectToPossibleExceptionHandler with and without a catch; mayThrowException's recursive branches; and computeFollowNode's many switch cases.

Since the real goal is branch coverage of this class, I can achieve it just by feeding process() various JS snippets that trigger each path, without needing deep assertions on CFG structure -- basic checks like non-null CFG and no thrown exceptions should suffice to catch gross faults, though I should still try to assert something meaningful where feasible to genuinely catch bugs.

To verify actual target identities for key transitions, I'll write a helper that collects the successor node values for a given DiGraphNode using cfg.getDirectedSuccNodes(), and since there's no direct lookup from an arbitrary AST node to its DiGraphNode, I'll instead search through cfg.getDirectedGraphNodes() to find the matching node by value.

With that lookup in place, I can now construct meaningful test assertions—parsing sample code like an if/else statement, running the control flow analysis, and checking that the CFG nodes correspond correctly to the parsed AST structure.

For actually running the analysis, I'm confirming the process call signature and reasoning through how the entry node gets computed for a script root—since SCRIPT isn't a DO/FOR/LABEL node, computeFallThrough should just return the script node itself as the entry point.

With traversal starting at root and visiting nodes post-order, the SCRIPT node gets visited last, triggering handleStmtList which creates the fallthrough edge to its first non-function child, matching what the test expects. I'm also trusting that parseTestCode returns the SCRIPT node directly rather than some wrapper, consistent with typical Closure Compiler test patterns.

Now I'm mapping out each if/else test case to the actual AST structure: for "if(a){b=1;}else{c=1;}" the IF node has three children (condition, then-block, else-block), so thenBlock is the condition's next sibling and elseBlock follows that, matching handleIf's logic exactly. For the case without an else clause, the IF node only has two children, so thenBlock.getNext() is null, meaning the ON_FALSE edge should point to whatever follows the IF statement via computeFollowNode -- which, since this is the only statement in the script, resolves to the implicit end.

Recursing once more with node=SCRIPT, parent becomes null, so the overall follow resolves to null, meaning the false edge from the if-node connects to the implicit return sentinel. That gives a solid test case: the successor set for ifNode should contain both the then-block and null.

I'm now working through similar cases for while, do-while, and for loops, checking that each loop's true-branch edge points to the body and its false-branch edge resolves to null when the loop is the last statement, and that do-while's fallthrough correctly targets the body block itself.

Writing test assertions...

I'm also considering the scenario where a switch has only a default case, no explicit case labels.

Then I move to the scenario where a case has neither a following case nor a default, verifying the false-branch edge points to the follow node after the switch, which is null when the switch is the last statement.

Now I'm starting on try-catch-finally handling, noting that the try node creates an unconditional edge to its first child block.

I need to trace how handleCatch works for the CATCH node, creating an unconditional edge to its last child (the catch body), and confirming the TRY node's structure — its second child is a BLOCK wrapping the CATCH node, matching the earlier check that compares NodeUtil.getCatchBlock(node) against the current node.

Adding member fields for compiler and root...

This assertion matches the source's handleTry logic directly since it just verifies the first-child edge target, so it works regardless of whether catch or finally exists. For the handleCatch test though, I'll need to figure out the exact tree shape to locate the CATCH node.

To avoid guessing the exact position, I'm writing a generic depth-first search helper that walks the tree using only confirmed API calls to find any node of a given type, then use it to locate the CATCH node and verify handleCatch's edge points from the catch node to its last child.

I plan to rely on this generic finder for CASE, DEFAULT_CASE, CATCH, BREAK, CONTINUE, FUNCTION, and similar node types instead of hard-coded positional navigation, though for IF, WHILE, and FOR I've already used direct positional access.

That means the break node's successor edge should point to null, which I'm now writing a test to verify by creating a labeled while loop with a break, finding the break node, and asserting its successors match this expectation.

testBreakWithoutTargetThrows()

Given the uncertainty, I'll settle for a safer test that just confirms process() completes without exceptions and cfg isn't null when shouldTraverseFunctions is false for a top-level function declaration, rather than asserting on exact branch behavior. I recall Closure's NodeTraversal checks shouldTraverse's return value to decide whether to descend into children, but I'm not certain if visit() still fires on the node itself when that returns false.

Actually this implies visit() must not be called when shouldTraverse returns false, contradicting my earlier assumption—otherwise that precondition would always fail for nested non-entry functions. Without the actual NodeTraversal source I can't be fully certain, but this failure mode strongly suggests skip-on-false is the real behavior.
